“We want to believe in our leaders. Society suffers when we do not. If we fear retribution and feel there is no choice but to live in blind obedience to those in power, we lose our way. We lose belief in our institutions. Good leaders are those who urge us to step up and demand justice and truth. They spark our imaginations with their visions of a better future. They educate us. Without a belief in the basic goodness of our leaders, we lose faith in ourselves and our collective future. Our standards and principles take a dive.

A leader is also great when they understand sacrifice and responsibility. This is why, I believe, people tune into ‘Star Trek’ or listen to Shakespeare, music or art of any kind. We are searching for hope and elevation from the daily numbness or despair. A desire to do good in the world works better with both kindness and focus — and it works better when we are surrounded by art and invention that lifts us. Jean-Luc Picard embodied that ideal. Patrick’s death means the loss of Picard, which for some hurts even more than the loss of Patrick Stewart. Jean-Luc gave us hope.”

अख्तियार दुरुपयोग अनुसन्धान आयोगले पूर्वप्रधानमन्त्री माधवकुमार नेपाल र नेपाली कांग्रेसका नेता तथा पूर्वमन्त्री डा. मिनेन्द्र रिजालसहितका व्यक्तिविरुद्ध भ्रष्टाचार मुद्दा दायर गरेको छ। सरकारी जग्गा गैरकानुनी रूपमा छुट दर्ता, सट्टापट्टा तथा बिक्री गरिएको आरोपमा अख्तियारले विशेष अदालतमा मुद्दा अघि बढाएको हो।

मोरङको विराटनगर र सुनसरीको इटहरी क्षेत्रसँग जोडिएको रिजाल क्यानिङ कम्पनी तथा रिजाल टासी इन्डस्ट्रिजको जग्गा प्रकरणमा अनियमितता भएको अख्तियारको दाबी छ।

अख्तियारका अनुसार कम्पनीको नाममा रहेको हदबन्दीभन्दा बढी जग्गा मन्त्रिपरिषद्को निर्णयमार्फत सट्टापट्टा गर्न अनुमति दिइएको थियो। त्यसपछि मूल्यवान् जग्गा बिक्री गरी अन्य स्थानको जग्गासँग सट्टापट्टा गरिएको विषयमा अनुसन्धान गरिएको हो।

तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री माधवकुमार नेपाल नेतृत्वको मन्त्रिपरिषद्ले गरेको निर्णय र त्यसमा तत्कालीन मन्त्री मिनेन्द्र रिजालको भूमिकालाई समेत अनुसन्धानको दायरामा ल्याइएको छ।

मन्त्रिपरिषद्को निर्णयमाथि प्रश्न

यो प्रकरणमा मन्त्रिपरिषद्बाट भएको निर्णयका आधारमा सार्वजनिक जग्गा व्यक्तिको स्वामित्वमा गएको वा कम्पनीलाई गैरकानुनी लाभ पुगेको भन्ने विषयमा अख्तियारले प्रश्न उठाएको छ।

आरोपपत्रमा तत्कालीन सरकारी अधिकारी, भूमि प्रशासनसँग सम्बन्धित कर्मचारी तथा जग्गा कारोबारमा संलग्न व्यक्तिहरूको भूमिकाबारे समेत अनुसन्धान गरिएको छ।

मुद्दामा पूर्वमन्त्री डम्बर श्रेष्ठ, पूर्वसचिव छविराज पन्त तथा भूमि व्यवस्थासँग सम्बन्धित अन्य उच्चपदस्थ अधिकारीहरू पनि प्रतिवादीको सूचीमा रहेको समाचार सार्वजनिक भएको छ।

९४ जना र ७६ करोडको प्रारम्भिक विवरण

मुद्दा दायर भएको सुरुवाती समाचारहरूमा माधव नेपाल र मिनेन्द्र रिजालसहित ९४ जनालाई प्रतिवादी बनाउँदै करिब ७६ करोड रुपैयाँ बिगो दाबी गरिएको उल्लेख थियो।

तर पछि सार्वजनिक भएका विवरणमा प्रतिवादीको संख्या र बिगो रकम फरक देखिएको छ। अनलाइनखबर र नागरिक न्यूजले ९७ जना प्रतिवादी तथा करिब ७३ करोड ४९ लाख रुपैयाँ बिगो दाबी गरिएको विवरण प्रकाशित गरेका छन्।

यस मुद्दामा केही व्यक्तिलाई जग्गा जफत गर्ने प्रयोजनका लागि मात्र विपक्षी बनाइएको समेत उल्लेख छ।

अदालतबाट हुन बाँकी छ अन्तिम फैसला

माधवकुमार नेपाल र मिनेन्द्र रिजालविरुद्ध भ्रष्टाचार मुद्दा दायर भए पनि उनीहरू दोषी प्रमाणित भइसकेका छैनन्। अख्तियारले लगाएका आरोप, प्रस्तुत प्रमाण र प्रतिवादीहरूको जवाफको परीक्षणपछि विशेष अदालतले निर्णय गर्नेछ।

बेलायत जाने नेपालीका लागि दुःखको खबर! पीआर पाउन १० वर्ष कुर्नुपर्ने!

अध्ययन, रोजगारी तथा स्थायी बसोबासको सपना बोकेर बेलायत जाने तयारीमा रहेका नेपालीहरूका लागि महत्त्वपूर्ण खबर सार्वजनिक भएको छ। बेलायत सरकारले विदेशी नागरिकलाई स्थायी बसोबास अनुमति अर्थात् पीआर प्राप्त गर्न लाग्ने समय बढाउने नयाँ नीति अघि सारेको छ। यसअनुसार अधिकांश विदेशी कामदारले अब पाँच वर्षको सट्टा १० वर्ष कुर्नुपर्ने व्यवस्था प्रस्ताव गरिएको छ।

बेलायतकी गृहमन्त्री शबाना महमुदले नोभेम्बर २ मा संसद्मा नयाँ अध्यागमन नीतिबारे जानकारी दिएकी हुन्। सरकारले यसलाई ‘अर्न्ड सेटलमेन्ट’ (Earned Settlement) नाम दिएको छ। यो व्यवस्थाअनुसार बेलायतमा कति वर्ष बसेको छ भन्ने मात्रै नभई व्यक्तिको आम्दानी, रोजगारी, आचरण तथा देशप्रतिको योगदानलाई पनि स्थायी बसोबासको आधार बनाइनेछ।

यसअघि बेलायतमा निश्चित प्रकारका कामदार भिसामा गएका विदेशी नागरिकले सामान्यतया पाँच वर्षपछि स्थायी बसोबासका लागि आवेदन दिन पाउने व्यवस्था थियो। तर नयाँ योजनाले अधिकांश कामदारका लागि उक्त अवधि दोब्बर बनाउनेछ।

सबैले १० वर्ष कुर्नुपर्ने भने होइन

बेलायत सरकारले सबै विदेशी नागरिकका लागि एउटै नियम लागू गर्ने भनेको छैन। वार्षिक ५० हजार पाउन्डभन्दा बढी आम्दानी भएका योग्य कामदार तथा डाक्टर, नर्स र शिक्षकजस्ता सार्वजनिक सेवाका केही कर्मचारीले पाँच वर्षमै स्थायी बसोबासका लागि आवेदन दिन सक्नेछन्।

त्यस्तै, वार्षिक एक लाख २५ हजार पाउन्डभन्दा बढी कमाउने उच्च आय भएका व्यक्तिले निश्चित सर्त पूरा गरे तीन वर्षमै स्थायी बसोबासको अवसर पाउन सक्नेछन्।

तर सामान्य आम्दानी भएका अधिकांश विदेशी कामदारले १० वर्ष कुर्नुपर्ने प्रस्ताव छ। अध्यागमन नियम उल्लङ्घन गर्ने व्यक्तिले भने अझ लामो समय कुर्नुपर्ने वा अनुमति नपाउन सक्ने व्यवस्था अघि सारिएको छ।

बेलायतमा रहेका नेपालीलाई कस्तो असर पर्छ?

बेलायतमा रोजगारी गरिरहेका तथा भविष्यमा त्यहाँ जाने तयारीमा रहेका नेपालीहरूलाई पनि नयाँ व्यवस्थाले असर पार्न सक्छ।

विशेषगरी सामान्य तलबमा काम गर्ने नेपालीहरूले स्थायी बसोबासका लागि पहिलेभन्दा लामो समय कुर्नुपर्ने अवस्था आउन सक्छ। यद्यपि, व्यक्तिको भिसाको प्रकार, पेशा, आम्दानी र अन्य योग्यताअनुसार फरक नियम लागू हुन सक्नेछन्।

बेलायत सरकारले यसअघि नै स्थायी बसोबास अनुमति प्राप्त गरिसकेका व्यक्तिको अधिकार नखोसिने स्पष्ट पारेको छ। साथै, केही स्वास्थ्य तथा हेरचाह सेवाका कामदार र बेलायतमा पहिल्यै बसोबास गरिरहेका व्यक्तिका लागि विशेष व्यवस्था पनि प्रस्ताव गरिएको छ।

सरकारी अनुमानअनुसार नयाँ नीतिका कारण पाँच लाखभन्दा बढी आप्रवासीले स्थायी बसोबास प्राप्त गर्न पहिलेभन्दा लामो समय कुर्नुपर्ने हुन सक्छ।

नयाँ नियम कहिलेदेखि लागू हुन्छ?

बेलायत सरकारले नयाँ नीति सार्वजनिक गरे पनि यसको विस्तृत कानुनी व्यवस्था र कार्यान्वयन प्रक्रिया अझै पूरा भएको छैन।

सरकारले डिसेम्बर २०२६ देखि अध्यागमन नियममा परिवर्तन अघि बढाउने र सन् २०२७ बाट चरणबद्ध रूपमा कार्यान्वयन गर्ने योजना सार्वजनिक गरेको छ।

नयाँ व्यवस्थाअनुसार स्थायी बसोबासका लागि आवेदन दिने व्यक्तिले आवश्यक अंग्रेजी भाषा ज्ञान, कानुनी आचरण, कर तथा राष्ट्रिय बीमामा योगदान र अन्य सरकारी मापदण्ड पूरा गर्नुपर्नेछ।

बेलायत सरकारले नयाँ नीतिले अध्यागमन प्रणालीलाई व्यवस्थित बनाउने र देशको अर्थतन्त्र तथा सार्वजनिक सेवामा योगदान गर्ने व्यक्तिलाई प्राथमिकता दिने दाबी गरेको छ।

सुरक्षाको चिन्ताबीच एसियाली खेलमा रोनाल्डो अनुपस्थित, प्रशिक्षकले दिए आराम!

पोर्चुगलका विश्वप्रसिद्ध फुटबलर क्रिस्टियानो रोनाल्डो एसियाली च्याम्पियन्स लिगअन्तर्गत उज्बेकिस्तानको पाख्ताकोरविरुद्धको खेलमा अनुपस्थित भएका छन्। मध्यपूर्वमा बढ्दो सुरक्षा चिन्ताका बीच साउदी अरेबियाको क्लब अल नासरका प्रशिक्षक एन्ज पोस्टेकोग्लुले रोनाल्डोलाई आराम दिने निर्णय गरेका हुन्।

नोभेम्बर २ मा उज्बेकिस्तानको राजधानी तास्कन्दमा भएको खेलका लागि रोनाल्डो टोलीसँग यात्रा गरेका थिएनन्। प्रशिक्षकले रोनाल्डोसँगै किङ्स्ले कोमान र मोहम्मद सिमाकानलाई पनि आराम दिएका थिए।

प्रशिक्षक पोस्टेकोग्लुका अनुसार लगातारको खेल तालिका, लामो यात्रा र खेलाडीहरूको शारीरिक अवस्थालाई ध्यानमा राख्दै उनीहरूलाई टोलीबाहिर राखिएको हो। त्यसैले रोनाल्डोको अनुपस्थितिलाई सुरक्षाका कारण मात्रै भएको निर्णयका रूपमा लिन मिल्दैन।

मध्यपूर्वको सुरक्षा अवस्थाले एसियाली फुटबल प्रभावित

पछिल्लो समय मध्यपूर्वमा देखिएको असुरक्षाले एसियाली फुटबल प्रतियोगिताहरूको सञ्चालनमा समेत असर पारेको छ। यसअघि अल नासर र संयुक्त अरब इमिरेट्सको क्लब अल वास्लबीच तय भएको खेल सुरक्षा चिन्ताका कारण स्थगित भएको थियो।

साउदी अरेबियामा भएका सुरक्षा घटनापछि अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय प्रतियोगिताका खेलाडी तथा टोलीहरूको यात्रालाई लिएर चिन्ता बढेको छ। यसले आगामी एसियाली फुटबल प्रतियोगिताहरूको व्यवस्थापनमा समेत चुनौती थपेको छ।

यसैबीच, साउदी अरेबियामा आयोजना हुने आगामी एसियन कपको सुरक्षा व्यवस्थाबारे पनि प्रश्न उठेका छन्। जापान फुटबल संघले समेत प्रतियोगिताको सुरक्षा अवस्थाप्रति चासो व्यक्त गरेको छ।

रोनाल्डोबिना अल नासरको शानदार जित

रोनाल्डो टोलीमा नभए पनि अल नासरले पाख्ताकोरलाई ६–२ गोलले पराजित गरेको छ। खेलमा पोर्चुगलका स्टार जोआओ फेलिक्सले दुई गोल गर्दै टोलीको जितमा महत्त्वपूर्ण योगदान दिएका थिए।

रोनाल्डो भने पछिल्लो समय उत्कृष्ट लयमा छन्। उनले साउदी प्रो लिगमा अल खोलूदविरुद्ध ह्याट्रिक गर्दै आफ्नो आधिकारिक करिअर गोलसंख्या ९८५ पुर्‍याएका थिए।

४१ वर्षीय रोनाल्डो अब ऐतिहासिक एक हजार गोलको उपलब्धिबाट केवल १५ गोल टाढा छन्। यही कारण उनको प्रत्येक खेल र गोलको प्रतीक्षा विश्वभरका समर्थकहरूले गरिरहेका छन्।

रोनाल्डोलाई पछि पार्दै हालान्ड बने विश्वकै सबैभन्दा बढी व्यावसायिक आकर्षण भएका फुटबलर!

नर्वेका स्टार स्ट्राइकर एर्लिङ हालान्डले पोर्चुगलका विश्वप्रसिद्ध फुटबलर क्रिस्टियानो रोनाल्डोलाई पछि पार्दै विश्वकै सबैभन्दा बढी व्यावसायिक आकर्षण भएका फुटबलरको स्थान हासिल गरेका छन्। खेलकुद व्यवसायसम्बन्धी अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय संस्था स्पोर्ट्सप्रो (SportsPro) ले सार्वजनिक गरेको सन् २०२६ को सूचीमा हालान्ड फुटबल खेलाडीमध्ये पहिलो स्थानमा परेका हुन्।

इंग्लिस क्लब म्यानचेस्टर सिटीबाट व्यावसायिक फुटबल खेल्दै आएका २६ वर्षीय हालान्ड विश्वका सबै खेलका सर्वाधिक व्यावसायिक आकर्षण भएका खेलाडीहरूको समग्र सूचीमा चौथो स्थानमा छन्। उनी फुटबल खेलाडीमध्ये शीर्ष १० मा पर्ने एकमात्र खेलाडी बनेका छन्।

यसैगरी, पोर्चुगलका कप्तान क्रिस्टियानो रोनाल्डो समग्र सूचीमा १४औँ स्थानमा परेका छन्। अघिल्लो वर्ष पाँचौँ स्थानमा रहेका रोनाल्डो यसपटक नौ स्थान तल झरेका हुन्।

स्पोर्ट्सप्रोले खेलाडीको ब्रान्ड मूल्य, लोकप्रियताको वृद्धि, विज्ञापन तथा प्रायोजनमा आकर्षण र भविष्यमा व्यावसायिक रूपमा विस्तार हुन सक्ने सम्भावनालाई आधार बनाएर सूची तयार गरेको हो।

हालान्डले कसरी पछि पारे रोनाल्डोलाई?

हालान्ड पछिल्ला वर्षहरूमा विश्व फुटबलका सबैभन्दा चर्चित स्ट्राइकरमध्ये एक बनेका छन्। म्यानचेस्टर सिटीका लागि उनको उत्कृष्ट प्रदर्शन, गोल गर्ने क्षमता र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय लोकप्रियताले मैदानबाहिर पनि उनको व्यावसायिक आकर्षण बढाएको छ।

स्पोर्ट्सप्रोका अनुसार हालान्डको लोकप्रियता गोल गर्ने क्षमतामा मात्रै सीमित छैन। उनको व्यक्तित्व, सामाजिक सञ्जालमा सक्रियता, मनोरञ्जनात्मक प्रस्तुति र युवा दर्शकसँगको सम्बन्धले पनि ब्रान्डहरूलाई आकर्षित गरेको छ।

अर्कोतर्फ, रोनाल्डोको विश्वव्यापी लोकप्रियता र स्थापित ब्रान्ड अझै बलियो छ। तर यस वर्षको मूल्यांकनमा भविष्यमा व्यावसायिक रूपमा विस्तार हुन सक्ने सम्भावनालाई विशेष महत्त्व दिइएकाले हालान्ड अगाडि देखिएका हुन्।

स्पोर्ट्सप्रोको १०० अंकको मूल्यांकन प्रणालीमा ब्रान्डको स्थापित शक्ति ४५ अंक, लोकप्रियताको गति ४० अंक र भविष्यको व्यावसायिक सम्भावना १५ अंकका आधारमा मूल्यांकन गरिएको थियो।

यस मूल्यांकनमा हालान्डले ७४.१८ अंक प्राप्त गर्दा रोनाल्डोले ६७.७२ अंक हासिल गरेका छन्।

मेसी, एम्बाप्पे र यामाल कति स्थानमा?

सूचीमा फ्रान्सका स्टार किलियन एम्बाप्पे १९औँ स्थानमा छन्। ब्राजिलका भिनिसियस जुनियर २०औँ स्थानमा रहँदा स्पेनका युवा स्टार लामिन यामाल २३औँ स्थानमा परेका छन्।

ब्राजिलका नेयमार २४औँ र अर्जेन्टिनाका विश्वविजेता कप्तान लियोनल मेसी २७औँ स्थानमा रहेका छन्।

समग्र सूचीको पहिलो स्थानमा बेलारुसकी टेनिस स्टार आरिना साबालेन्का रहेकी छन्। दोस्रो स्थानमा चिनियाँ फ्रिस्टाइल स्की खेलाडी आइलीन गु र तेस्रो स्थानमा बास्केटबल स्टार यानिस एन्टेटोकुन्म्पो रहेका छन्।

स्पोर्ट्सप्रोले ७० खेलका १ हजार २०२ खेलाडीलाई अध्ययनको प्रारम्भिक दायरामा राखेर सूची तयार गरेको हो। यसमा खेलाडीहरूको सामाजिक सञ्जालको प्रभाव, दर्शकको चासो, ब्रान्डसँगको साझेदारी र व्यावसायिक सम्भावनालगायतका पक्ष मूल्यांकन गरिएको थियो।

रास्वपाका सांसद यज्ञमणि न्यौपानेका अनुसार महाभियोग प्रक्रिया अघि बढाउन दुईवटा विकल्पमाथि तयारी भइरहेको छ। पहिलो, प्रतिनिधिसभाका तीन जना सांसदले संघीय संसद्का महासचिव वा सचिवसमक्ष महाभियोगको सूचना दर्ता गराउने। दोस्रो, प्रतिनिधिसभाका एक चौथाइ सांसदले महाभियोग प्रस्ताव दर्ता गर्ने।

तीन सांसदले सूचना दिएमा महाभियोग सिफारिस समितिले त्यसबारे अध्ययन गर्नेछ। समितिको प्रक्रिया र सिफारिसपछि प्रतिनिधिसभामा आवश्यक समर्थन जुटेमा महाभियोगको प्रक्रिया अघि बढ्न सक्नेछ।

त्यस्तै, प्रतिनिधिसभाको नियमावलीअनुसार एक चौथाइ सांसदले महाभियोग प्रस्ताव दर्ता गराएमा १५ दिनभित्र बैठक बस्ने गरी संसद् अधिवेशन आह्वान गर्नुपर्ने व्यवस्था छ। यस्तो प्रस्ताव दर्ता भएपछि सम्बन्धित न्यायाधीश निलम्बनमा पर्ने कानुनी प्रावधानसमेत छ।

अहिले तिहार र छठजस्ता पर्वका कारण तत्काल संसद् अधिवेशन बोलाउन कठिन हुने तथा सरकारले मंसिर दोस्रो सातातिर अधिवेशन आह्वान गर्ने तयारी गरेको बताइएको छ। त्यसैले रास्वपाले तीन जना सांसदले महाभियोगको सूचना दिने विकल्पबाट प्रक्रिया अघि बढाउन सक्ने सम्भावना बढी रहेको समाचारमा उल्लेख छ।

महाभियोगका लागि कुन विधि अपनाउने भन्ने विषय भने संसदीय दलको बैठक र आवश्यक परामर्शपछि टुंगो लाग्नेछ।

उत्तर कोरियाले बनायो नयाँ घातक हतियार क्लस्टर वारहेड! एउटै मिसाइलले ६ हेक्टर क्षेत्र ध्वस्त पार्न सक्ने!

उत्तर कोरियाले नयाँ शक्तिशाली क्लस्टर वारहेडसहितको क्रुज मिसाइल परीक्षण गरेको घोषणा गरेको छ। उत्तर कोरियाली सरकारी सञ्चारमाध्यमका अनुसार उक्त हतियारले एउटै आक्रमणमा ५ देखि ६ हेक्टरसम्मको क्षेत्र ध्वस्त पार्न सक्ने दाबी गरिएको छ। पछिल्लो परीक्षणसँगै उत्तर कोरियाको सैन्य क्षमता र हतियार विकास कार्यक्रम फेरि अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय चर्चामा आएको छ।

उत्तर कोरियाको सरकारी समाचार संस्था केसीएनएले मंगलबार सार्वजनिक गरेको विवरणअनुसार नोभेम्बर २ मा रणनीतिक क्रुज मिसाइलमा जडान गरिएको नयाँ क्लस्टर वारहेडको प्रभावकारिता परीक्षण गरिएको हो। परीक्षणको उद्देश्य नयाँ हतियारको क्षमता र मिसाइलको उडानसम्बन्धी विशेषता मूल्यांकन गर्नु रहेको बताइएको छ।

उत्तर कोरियाली मिसाइल प्रशासनअन्तर्गतको वारहेड अनुसन्धान संस्थानले नयाँ मध्यम आकारको क्लस्टर वारहेडले एकैपटक ठूलो क्षेत्र प्रभावित पार्न सक्ने दाबी गरेको छ। यद्यपि, उत्तर कोरियाले सार्वजनिक गरेको उक्त क्षमताको स्वतन्त्र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय पुष्टि भने भएको छैन।

क्लस्टर वारहेड यस्तो प्रकारको हतियार हो, जसले एउटै मिसाइलबाट धेरै साना विस्फोटक सामग्री विभिन्न स्थानमा फैलाउन सक्छ। यसका कारण एकैपटक ठूलो क्षेत्र प्रभावित हुन सक्ने भएकाले यस्ता हतियारको प्रयोगलाई लिएर अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय स्तरमा गम्भीर मानवीय तथा सुरक्षा चिन्ता रहँदै आएको छ।

पछिल्लो परीक्षणको निरीक्षण उत्तर कोरियाको सत्तारूढ वर्कर्स पार्टीको केन्द्रीय सैन्य आयोगका सदस्य जनरल किम जोङ-सिकले गरेको समाचारमा उल्लेख छ। तर उत्तर कोरियाली नेता किम जोङ-उन स्वयं परीक्षणस्थलमा उपस्थित थिए भन्ने जानकारी सार्वजनिक गरिएको छैन।

उत्तर कोरियाले यसअघि अक्टोबर ३१ मा पनि रणनीतिकभन्दा फरक प्रकारको ब्यालिस्टिक मिसाइलमा प्रयोग गर्न सकिने क्लस्टर वारहेड परीक्षण गरेको थियो। उक्त परीक्षणमा १२ देखि १३ हेक्टरसम्मको क्षेत्र प्रभावित पार्न सक्ने दाबी गरिएको थियो।

लगातार भइरहेका यी परीक्षणलाई उत्तर कोरियाले आफ्नो रक्षा क्षमता सुदृढ गर्ने प्रयासका रूपमा प्रस्तुत गरेको छ। उत्तर कोरियाली अधिकारीहरूले बाह्य सुरक्षा चुनौतीहरूको सामना गर्न आधुनिक हतियार प्रणालीको विकास आवश्यक रहेको बताएका छन्।

उत्तर कोरियाले सन् २०२६ को अन्त्यसम्म विभिन्न प्रकारका क्लस्टर वारहेड सैन्य प्रयोगका लागि उपलब्ध गराउने लक्ष्यसमेत सार्वजनिक गरेको छ।

यसैबीच, उत्तर कोरियाको लगातारको मिसाइल परीक्षणले कोरियाली प्रायद्वीपको सुरक्षा अवस्थाबारे नयाँ चिन्ता उत्पन्न गरेको छ। दक्षिण कोरिया र अमेरिकाले उत्तर कोरियाको सैन्य गतिविधिलाई नजिकबाट निगरानी गर्दै आएका छन्।

A deadly helicopter accident occurred in Nepal’s Khumbu region of Solukhumbu district on Tuesday morning after two helicopters belonging to Fishtail Air and Dynasty Air collided mid-air. The accident took place at around 8:11 AM in Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality-4, killing one Indian tourist and injuring three others.

According to Solukhumbu police, the deceased has been identified as Indian national Vasant Kumar Balaramaramadu, who was travelling aboard the Fishtail Air helicopter. His body was taken to a hospital in Lukla.

Another passenger, Shailesh Krishna Patel, a New Zealand citizen of Indian origin, was injured and airlifted to Mediciti Hospital in Kathmandu for treatment. Both helicopters' pilots also sustained minor injuries and were brought to Kathmandu for further medical care.

Authorities have yet to disclose what caused the two helicopters to collide. Further details about the accident are awaited.

नेकपा एमालेका नेता सूर्य थापाले प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाहकी पत्नी सविना काफ्लेको पहिरनलाई लिएर व्यंग्यात्मक टिप्पणी गरेका छन्। उनले काफ्लेको पहिरनलाई पञ्चायतकालमा चर्चामा रहेको ‘पम्फादेवी’ प्रसंगसँग जोड्दै सामाजिक सञ्जालमा टिप्पणी गरेका हुन्।

प्रधानमन्त्री पत्नी काफ्ले हालै एक कार्यक्रममा रेड कार्पेटमा हिँडेको तस्बिर सामाजिक सञ्जालमा भाइरल भइरहेको छ। सोही तस्बिर फेसबुकमा राख्दै थापाले उनको निलो सल र पहिरनबारे कटाक्ष गरेका छन्।

थापाले पञ्चायतकालको अन्त्यतिर ‘पम्फादेवी’ को मुजा पछाडि पारेर सारी लगाएको विषय चर्चामा रहेको स्मरण गराउँदै अहिले निलो सल लगाउने नयाँ भेरियन्ट देखिएको टिप्पणी गरेका छन्।

उनले लेखेका छन्, ‘अहिले निलो सल लगाउँदै हिँड्ने नयाँ भेरियन्ट सार्वजनिक भयो। महेन्द्रको नक्कल गर्दै रिमिक्समा गोल्डस्टार सेतो जुत्ता, कालो टिसर्ट र कोट लगाएर संसदमा जाने अभ्यास त छँदै थियो। रातो कार्पेटमा यो निलो सल लतार्दै खच्याङखच्याङ हिँड्ने पनि पम्फादेवीकै नक्कल हो कि अरू कसैको प्रभाव छ?’

थापाले प्रधानमन्त्री र ‘फर्स्ट लेडी’ को पहिरनका लागि निश्चित ड्रेसकोड हुनुपर्ने मान्यताका आधारमा यस्तो टिप्पणी गरेको बताएका छन्।
को हुन् पम्फादेवी?
पञ्चायतकालमा ‘पम्फादेवी’ नाम तत्कालीन रानी ऐश्वर्यसँग जोडिएर चर्चामा आउने गरेको थियो। विशेषगरी दरबारको शक्ति, प्रभाव र आर्थिक अपारदर्शितासम्बन्धी आरोप तथा चर्चामा यो नाम प्रयोग हुने गरेको थियो।

पञ्चायतको अन्तिम समय र २०४६ सालको जनआन्दोलनका क्रममा ‘पम्फादेवी’ नाम निकै चर्चित बनेको थियो। तत्कालीन दरबारको आर्थिक गतिविधि र शक्तिको दुरुपयोगबारे उठेका आरोपसँग यो नाम जोडिने गरेको थियो। रानी ऐश्वर्यले स्विट्जरल्यान्डको बैंकमा ‘पम्फादेवी’ नाममा ठूलो रकम राखेको भन्ने हल्लासमेत फैलिएको थियो। पञ्चायतविरोधी आन्दोलनका क्रममा ‘पम्फादेवी मुर्दावाद’ जस्ता नारा पनि लाग्ने गरेका थिए।

यद्यपि, स्विस बैंकमा उक्त नाममा ठूलो रकम रहेको भन्ने दाबी पुष्टि गर्ने ठोस सार्वजनिक प्रमाण उपलब्ध छैन।

नेपाल सरकारले सडक निर्माणमा नयाँ नीति अघि सारेको छ। प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाह (बालेन) नेतृत्वको सरकारले विदेशबाट आयात गरिने बिटुमिन अर्थात् अलकत्राको विकल्पमा नेपालमै उत्पादित सिमेन्ट प्रयोग गरेर सडक निर्माण गर्ने योजनालाई प्राथमिकता दिएको हो।

सरकारले ‘सार्वजनिक खरिदमा स्वदेशी उत्पादनको प्रवर्द्धन र प्रयोगसम्बन्धी निर्देशिका, २०८३’ स्वीकृत गरेसँगै सडक निर्माणमा स्वदेशी सिमेन्टको प्रयोग बढाउने बाटो खुलेको छ। यस निर्णयले नेपालका सिमेन्ट उद्योगलाई प्रोत्साहन गर्नुका साथै विदेशबाट आयात हुने निर्माण सामग्रीमाथिको निर्भरता घटाउने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ।

विशेषगरी पहाडी क्षेत्रका उकालो, घुमाउरो सडक, ओसिलो स्थान तथा कालोपत्रे छिट्टै बिग्रिने क्षेत्रमा सिमेन्टबाट सडक निर्माणलाई प्राथमिकता दिइने भएको छ। त्यस्ता स्थानमा कंक्रिट सडक बढी टिकाउ हुन सक्ने सरकारी अधिकारीहरूको भनाइ छ।

यसअघि नेपालमा अधिकांश सडक निर्माणका लागि विदेशबाट आयात गरिएको बिटुमिन प्रयोग गरिँदै आएको थियो। तर अब सरकारले स्वदेशमै उपलब्ध गुणस्तरीय सिमेन्ट तथा अन्य निर्माण सामग्री प्रयोग बढाउने नीति लिएको छ।

सरकारको नयाँ व्यवस्थाअनुसार सडक, पुल तथा सरकारी भवनका आयोजना डिजाइन गर्दादेखि नै उपयुक्त स्वदेशी सामग्रीलाई प्राथमिकता दिनुपर्नेछ। बोलपत्र तथा निर्माण सम्झौतामा समेत स्वदेशी सामग्री प्रयोगसम्बन्धी व्यवस्था समावेश गरिनेछ।

सिमेन्ट सडक निर्माणमा कति खर्च लाग्छ?

नेपाल निर्माण व्यवसायी महासंघले उपलब्ध गराएको लागत विवरणअनुसार साढे पाँच मिटर चौडाइको एक किलोमिटर अस्फाल्ट कालोपत्रे सडक निर्माण गर्न करिब १ करोड ७७ लाख रुपैयाँ लाग्छ। सोही आकारको सिमेन्ट कंक्रिट सडक निर्माण गर्दा करिब ३ करोड ५ लाख रुपैयाँ खर्च हुने अनुमान छ।

सिमेन्ट सडकको सुरुवाती निर्माण लागत बढी भए पनि लामो समय टिक्न सक्ने र मर्मतमा लाग्ने खर्च घट्न सक्ने भएकाले यसको प्रयोग बढाउनुपर्ने निर्माण व्यवसायीहरूको भनाइ छ।

यद्यपि, सरकारले देशभरका सबै सडक एकैपटक सिमेन्टबाट बनाउने निर्णय भने गरेको छैन। प्राविधिक रूपमा उपयुक्त र आवश्यक देखिएका स्थानमा मात्रै सिमेन्ट कंक्रिट सडक निर्माण गरिनेछ।

सरकारले सिमेन्ट सडक निर्माणका लागि छुट्टै बोलपत्र आह्वान गर्ने तयारीसमेत अघि बढाएको छ। निर्माण अघि नै प्राविधिक अध्ययन गरेर कुन सडकमा कुन सामग्री उपयुक्त हुन्छ भन्ने निर्धारण गरिनेछ।

एसपी कार्कीका अनुसार गृहमन्त्री गुरुङविरुद्ध फेसबुकमा स्टाटस लेखेको विषयमा उजुरी परेको भन्दै गोरखा प्रहरीले पक्राउ गर्न पत्र पठाएको थियो। सोही पत्रका आधारमा अधिकारीलाई पक्राउ गरेर गोरखा पठाइएको उनले बताए।

अधिकारीले पछिल्ला केही दिनदेखि प्रधानमन्त्री शाह र गृहमन्त्री गुरुङलाई लक्षित गर्दै फेसबुकमा विभिन्न स्टाटस लेख्दै आएका थिए। गृहमन्त्री गुरुङलाई गोरखाबाट लखेटेको आशयको स्टाटस लेखेपछि उनीमाथि कारबाही गर्नुपर्ने भन्दै उजुरी परेको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ।

केही दिनअघि गृहमन्त्री गुरुङ मतदातासँग भेटघाट गर्न र सचिवालय उद्घाटनका लागि गोरखा पुगेका थिए।

सरकारले देशभर एउटै ब्रान्डको एलपी ग्यास सिलिन्डर लागू गर्ने तयारी थालेको छ। बजारमा विभिन्न कम्पनीका सिलिन्डर प्रयोग भइरहँदा उपभोक्ताले ग्यास सकिएपछि अर्को ब्रान्डको सिलिन्डरसँग साट्न समस्या भोग्दै आएका छन्। यही समस्या समाधान गर्ने उद्देश्यले सरकारले एउटै ब्रान्डको सिलिन्डर प्रणाली लागू गर्ने तयारी अघि बढाएको हो।

हाल नेपालमा ५८ वटा विभिन्न ब्रान्डका एलपी ग्यास सिलिन्डर बजारमा प्रयोग भइरहेका छन्। फरक–फरक कम्पनीका सिलिन्डर भएकै कारण उपभोक्ताले एउटा ब्रान्डको सिलिन्डर लिएर अर्को ब्रान्डको ग्यास पसलमा जाँदा साट्न नपाउने वा थप झन्झट व्यहोर्नुपर्ने अवस्था छ।

विशेषगरी एउटा कम्पनीको ग्यास प्रयोग गर्ने उपभोक्ताले अर्को कम्पनीको ग्यास पसलबाट सिलिन्डर साट्न नपाउँदा खाली सिलिन्डर बोकेर सम्बन्धित कम्पनीको डिलर खोज्नुपर्ने बाध्यता छ। एउटै ब्रान्ड लागू भएमा यस्तो समस्या हट्ने र ग्यास वितरण तथा आपूर्तिमा सहजता आउने सरकारको अपेक्षा छ।

यद्यपि, एउटै ब्रान्डको सिलिन्डर लागू गर्ने योजना कसरी कार्यान्वयन गर्ने, हाल बजारमा रहेका ५८ ब्रान्डका सिलिन्डरको व्यवस्थापन कसरी गर्ने र ग्यास उद्योगहरूलाई कसरी समेट्ने भन्ने विषयमा थप तयारी आवश्यक हुनेछ। सरकारले यस योजनालाई कार्यान्वयनमा ल्याउन सके एलपी ग्यास प्रयोग गर्ने देशभरका उपभोक्तालाई प्रत्यक्ष राहत पुग्ने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ।

अनुसन्धानअनुसार लालीगुराँस पशुपालन फार्मबाट मात्रै कर्मचारीको खातामा चार करोड ४२ लाख रुपैयाँ आएको छ । दुर्घटनामा मृत्यु भएका रितेश राय यादवको खातामा विभिन्न कृषि फार्मबाट दुई करोड ७८ लाख रुपैयाँ जम्मा भएको देखिएको छ । त्यस्तै रामकेवल रायको खातामा एक करोड १४ लाख र उनका छोरा जितेन्द्रकुमार यादवको खातामा एक करोड ३२ लाख रुपैयाँ आएको सिआइबीको अनुसन्धानमा उल्लेख छ ।

यसैगरी, कर्मचारी मनहरि शर्माको खातामा एक करोड १५ लाख, शिवनन्द रायको खातामा एक करोड ६९ लाख र नवीन राय यादवले एक करोड ९३ लाख रुपैयाँ लिएको अनुसन्धानबाट खुलेको छ । तत्कालीन महाप्रबन्धक झाको कार्यकालमा मात्रै पाँच करोड रुपैयाँ घोटाला भएको सिआइबीको दाबी छ ।

Just a few years ago, thousands of migrants, including families with children, gathered at the Poland-Belarus border, hoping to enter the European Union.

The Polish government says its border security measures have successfully reduced illegal crossings and protected national security. Officials have also accused Belarus of using migration as a tool to destabilise the European Union.

Thousands of Strangers Become Family at Chinese Groom’s Wedding

A 24-year-old Chinese man who feared his wedding would be almost empty ended up celebrating with thousands of strangers after a heartfelt social media invitation went viral.

Xu Chenghong, who lost his father at age three and his grandmother at seven, grew up with very few close family members. After years of hard work, he finally saved enough to marry his girlfriend, but feared that only a handful of guests would attend.

Hoping to make the day less lonely, he posted an invitation on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, asking strangers to join his wedding. He expected around 10 to 20 people to show up.

Instead, thousands of people reportedly travelled from across China to celebrate with the couple. Some brought livestock, food and household appliances, while volunteer chefs prepared meals and supporters helped organise the event. A Maybach was even arranged for the newlyweds.

The overwhelming response forced organisers to move the celebration to a larger venue, with local authorities helping manage the crowds.

What began as a simple request for a few wedding guests became an extraordinary celebration of kindness, proving that family is not always defined by blood, but by the people who show up when it matters most.

Too Much Screen Time in Schools? Sweden Is Changing Its Education Strategy

Sweden is rethinking its technology-driven education strategy after growing concerns about the impact of excessive screen use on children's learning. Once among the countries enthusiastically introducing laptops and tablets into classrooms, Sweden is now shifting its focus back towards printed textbooks, handwriting and traditional reading.

The change follows concerns over declining reading performance among fourth-grade students between 2016 and 2021. Educators and researchers have raised questions about children's concentration, reading comprehension and dependence on digital devices. In response, Sweden has invested more than 2.1 billion Swedish kronor in printed textbooks and teacher guides.

The country has also changed its approach to early childhood education, with preschools no longer required to use digital tools. More classroom time is being directed towards reading physical books and practising handwriting, while a nationwide mobile phone ban in schools is planned.

However, Sweden's shift does not mean completely rejecting technology. Digital skills remain important for children's future, but policymakers are increasingly recognising that screens are not necessarily the best learning tool for every age group or subject. The country's experience highlights an important lesson for education systems worldwide: technological innovation should support learning, not replace the fundamentals of reading, writing and focused attention.

The real story: Two female belugas with marked spinal deformities washed ashore on the banks of the St. Lawrence River in Quebec and were examined at the Université de Montréal's Faculty of Veterinary Medicine with CT scans. Both were emaciated. In the first, a 17-year-old female, arthritis caused by the deformities likely contributed to her death. Source: Canadian Wildlife Health Cooperative (CWHC-Quebec), published 2026.

Researchers who watch St. Lawrence belugas from boats had seen it before: now and then, a living whale with a visibly bent spine. What nobody had done was examine one up close. Then two female belugas with marked spinal deformities washed ashore on the banks of the river, and the Quebec team of the Canadian Wildlife Health Cooperative finally had the chance.

Both whales were taken to the Université de Montréal's Faculty of Veterinary Medicine for post-mortem examination and computed tomography scans. Both were emaciated. In the first, a 17-year-old young adult female, the scientists found significant degenerative osteoarthritis secondary to the spinal deformities. They concluded that these bone malformations ultimately contributed to her death, most likely by making it harder for her to move and feed.

The finding is both small and large. A preliminary review of photographs of living belugas collected since 2003 by the Group for Research and Education on Marine Mammals suggests that vertebral deformities are present in fewer than 3 percent of the whales photographed. What causes them is still not known; the researchers say the two examinations "pave the way" for further investigation. For a population already struggling to raise calves, every animal that can't hunt properly is another loss, and a question still waiting for an answer.

Picture a man sitting on a live, armed ejection seat that could fire at any instant and throw him out through a missing hatch, and picture him trapped there for about 25 minutes, aboard a burning bomber, while the rest of his crew flew it toward an emergency landing, with him still on board. They did it because they had decided no one was leaving without him.

It happened on May 1, 2018. A B-1B Lancer from Dyess Air Force Base, Texas, was returning from a training flight when an engine caught fire. The crew ran the checklist; the fire wouldn't go out. The last step was to eject. The commander gave the order, and the offensive systems operator went first, the hatch above him blew clear, but his ejection seat failed to fire. Suddenly he was trapped on an armed seat that could go off at any second, even on landing.

Within about two seconds, the aircraft commander called off the ejection. As the Secretary of the Air Force later recounted his words: "We are going to try for all of us to make it, rather than sacrifice the one guy who can't get out."

On fire, missing a hatch, open to the wind, they flew more than 150 miles and landed the crippled bomber at Midland, Texas. All four men walked away unhurt. Each received the Distinguished Flying Cross. "No one left behind" isn't just a saying. On that day, a young crew kept it.

They once doubted he'd ever amount to much as a leader. Then, on August 7, 1942, Major General Alexander Vandegrift took the 1st Marine Division ashore at Guadalcanal — America's first major ground offensive against Japan — and held it through months of hunger, disease, and relentless enemy assaults around Henderson Field.

His leadership earned him the Medal of Honor, and his career was just getting started: he went on to become Commandant of the Marine Corps and, in 1945, the first Marine on active duty to wear four stars. Guadalcanal turned the tide of the Pacific War. The doubters were wrong — and history proved it.

Operating at the tip of the spear for JSOC's direct-action elements—spearheaded under Task Force 20 and later Task Force 121 / Task Force 145—Delta squadrons executed relentless nighttime raids across Iraq dismantling high-value Ba'athist regime targets and emerging Al-Qaeda in Iraq networks.

Pictured here on a captured Iraqi airfield in front of destroyed Iraqi Air Force transport aircraft, the team embodies early-2000s direct-action culture: modified tri-color desert DCU trousers, customized rattle-can spray-painted M4A1 carbines, early Aimpoint CompM2 optics, PEQ-2 infrared lasers, and sound suppressors.

Tu Lam was born in Saigon in December 1974, just months before the city fell. As a small child, he escaped Vietnam with his family on a crowded wooden fishing boat, surviving pirates, starvation, and days at sea before reaching a refugee camp in Indonesia. In 1981, the family settled in North Carolina, where he grew up facing racism and poverty, and made a promise to himself that he was stronger than hate.

He kept that promise. Lam joined the Army and spent 23 years in uniform, 20 of them as a Green Beret, deploying to conflicts around the world. His career also took him into the Army's SMU community as an augmentee, and he retired as a Master Sergeant.

After leaving the military, he founded Ronin Tactics, built on his combat experience, his lifelong study of martial arts, and the samurai code of bushido. He became the inspiration for the character Ronin in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare, co-hosted Forged in Fire: Knife or Death, and told his story in his memoir, "The Way of Ronin."

It's one of the most improbable images in the history of air combat: one fighter jet, over enemy territory, physically pushing another crippled jet through the sky to keep it flying. It really happened, on March 10, 1967, over North Vietnam, and it's remembered as Pardo's Push.

He and his backseater were about to go down deep in enemy territory. His wingman, Captain Bob Pardo, refused to let that happen.

Pardo had Aman lower his tailhook, the steel hook used to catch wires on a carrier, then eased it against the glass of his own windshield and began to push. Aman shut down his engines. For about 20 minutes, one Phantom flew two, the hook slipping off every few seconds, Pardo repositioning and pushing again, until he'd driven the dying jet some 80 miles into Laos. Then his own engine caught fire and he ejected too.

All four men were rescued within two hours. Pardo's reward at first was a reprimand for risking the aircraft. It took 22 years before he got the Silver Star. He never called it heroism, he just refused to leave his wingman behind.

Aerodynamic & Forensic Breakdown
The In-Flight Breakup Finding: During their initial media briefing in Palm Beach County, NTSB investigators confirmed that the Learjet 60 began shedding components prior to striking the ground, officially expanding the search radius across residential neighborhoods miles away from the primary impact crater.

The Missing Horizontal Stabilizer: Close-up frame analysis of civilian dashcam footage captured seconds before impact appears to show the aircraft's T-tail fuselage cleanly sheared off, missing the entire horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly that controls aircraft pitch.

Why Loss of the Stabilizer is Fatal: On swept-wing, T-tail jets like the Learjet 60, the horizontal stabilizer generates continuous downward aerodynamic force to counter the natural forward center of gravity. If the stabilizer separates due to severe structural flutter, pitch trim runaway, or aerodynamic over-stress, the aircraft immediately lawn-darts into a near-vertical terminal dive that is physically impossible to pull out of, regardless of pilot yoke input.

The Escalating Mayday Telemetry: Flight tracking telemetry and ATC recordings show the crew encountered severe weather and icing while climbing through 8,700 feet. The aircraft suddenly entered an uncontrollable overspeed condition, with vertical descent rates accelerating from 10,000 FPM past 32,000 FPM before the violent ground collision.

Locating the Empennage Components: Ground teams are prioritizing the recovery of tail structure fragments, elevator control horns, and pitch trim actuators to determine whether failure was aerodynamic, mechanical, or structural.

Analyzing Trim Jackscrew Position: Recovery crews will inspect the horizontal stabilizer trim actuator jackscrew to determine if an uncommanded runaway pitch condition preceded the structural separation.

Evaluating Atmospheric Stress & Icing: Meteorologists and investigators are analyzing weather radar data to evaluate whether severe convective turbulence or structural ice accumulation induced catastrophic aerodynamic loading at cruise altitude.

When the Civil War broke out, Mary Walker wasn't asking for permission. She was already a doctor, one of the very few women in America who could say that back in 1855. The Army told her women couldn't serve as surgeons. So she showed up anyway and worked for free.

She treated wounded Union soldiers in field hospitals, often close to the fighting. She'd cross into dangerous ground to care for civilians too, and in April 1864 that cost her. Confederate troops captured her and accused her of being a spy. She spent four months locked up in Castle Thunder prison in Richmond before she was traded back in a prisoner exchange.

In November 1865, President Andrew Johnson awarded her the Medal of Honor.

But her story didn't end neatly. In 1917, the government tightened the rules and took the medal back from her and hundreds of others. Mary's answer? She refused to return it. She wore it every single day until she died in 1919.

It took almost 60 more years, but in 1977 President Jimmy Carter restored her medal.

To this day, she is the only woman ever to receive the Medal of Honor.

Prisoners of war have tried everything to escape, but few plans were as patient — or as strange — as Benjamin Purcell's. Held in a North Vietnamese prison camp, the Army officer spent months secretly drilling tiny holes into his cell door, a little at a time, always watching for the guards. His early-warning system was a chicken he had trained to react whenever anyone approached.

Picture the fastest jet ever built sitting on the runway, dripping. Before every mission, the SR-71 Blackbird leaked fuel onto the concrete, puddles of it spreading beneath the plane while the ground crew worked, completely unbothered. It looked like something was badly wrong. Nothing was. The leaking was deliberate, and it's one of the most ingenious stories in aviation.

The reason is heat. The Blackbird cruised faster than 2,000 mph, and air friction alone heated its skin to hundreds of degrees. Metal expands when it's that hot, so Lockheed built the fuselage and fuel tanks with deliberate gaps, loose on the ground, sealing tight only once the plane heated and stretched several inches longer in flight. On the cold ground, those gaps sat open, and the fuel seeped out. So the Blackbird took off light, then refueled from a tanker once airborne and sealed.

The fuel itself was so hard to ignite you could reportedly drop a lit match in it and it would go out. And the ultimate irony: to survive Mach 3 heat, the plane was about 85% titanium, which the US couldn't supply, so the CIA secretly bought it from the Soviet Union, the very country the SR-71 was built to spy on.

Retired in the 1990s, never officially replaced. The puddle under its wings wasn't a flaw. It was the signature of genius.

“WE WERE STACKING SO MANY BODIES THAT PATROLS HAD TO GO OUT TO MOVE THEM OFF OUR FIELDS OF FIRE.” — Marine Raider Cody Alford on the Battle of Fallujah on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most intense firsthand accounts of modern urban warfare ever recorded on The Shawn Ryan Show, former Marine Raider and Scout Sniper Cody Alford broke down the brutal house-to-house meatgrinder of Operation Phantom Fury—and the terrifying out-of-body experience he suffered after taking an insurgent sniper bullet directly to the helmet.

In his own words:

“The night prior to going in, my platoon commander walks in and says, ‘Everyone is going to write their death letter.’

I’m 18 years old, sitting there thinking: What do you even write? I wrote a letter to my girlfriend, wrote one to my parents, turned them over to the platoon commander, and that’s when I knew shit was real.

In Fallujah, the brutality of what we were up against was beyond comprehension. The human shields, the mutilations, the sheer volume of combat. We were stacking so many bodies that we had to send patrols out into the street just to drag bodies out of the way because they were blocking our fields of fire.

I remember stepping behind a window frame, slamming in a fresh magazine, and as soon as I pop out to shoot, everything goes black.

A profound exhale left my body, and I hit the deck. That’s when I had this out-of-body experience. It was like a video game glitch—a top-down view looking down at the entire scene. I could see the fighters across the street. I could see my own body lying still. I could see my point man still firing. I saw this blinding light, thinking: I’m f**king dead.

Then suddenly, I got sucked back into my body. I came to curled up in a fetal position with my buddy kicking my leg shouting, ‘Wake up! We thought you were dead!’

The bullet had hit me flush in the helmet.”

The Second Battle of Fallujah stands as the bloodiest, most relentless urban combat the U.S. Marine Corps has fought since the Battle of Huế City in 1968.

“EVIDENCE INDICATES PARTS OF THE JET BROKE OFF BEFORE IMPACT.” — Federal investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board reveal that the doomed Learjet 60 that crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, likely suffered an in-flight structural breakup at altitude, aligning with dashcam video appearing to show the aircraft plunging nose-first without its T-tail horizontal stabilizer.

“There are indications the aircraft began breaking up prior to impact. We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site... We are asking anyone in the community who locates debris to contact local law enforcement immediately.”

Aerodynamic & Forensic Breakdown
The In-Flight Breakup Finding: During their initial media briefing in Palm Beach County, NTSB investigators confirmed that the Learjet 60 began shedding components prior to striking the ground, officially expanding the search radius across residential neighborhoods miles away from the primary impact crater.

The Missing Horizontal Stabilizer: Close-up frame analysis of civilian dashcam footage captured seconds before impact appears to show the aircraft's T-tail fuselage cleanly sheared off, missing the entire horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly that controls aircraft pitch.

Why Loss of the Stabilizer is Fatal: On swept-wing, T-tail jets like the Learjet 60, the horizontal stabilizer generates continuous downward aerodynamic force to counter the natural forward center of gravity. If the stabilizer separates due to severe structural flutter, pitch trim runaway, or aerodynamic over-stress, the aircraft immediately lawn-darts into a near-vertical terminal dive that is physically impossible to pull out of, regardless of pilot yoke input.

The Escalating Mayday Telemetry: Flight tracking telemetry and ATC recordings show the crew encountered severe weather and icing while climbing through 8,700 feet. The aircraft suddenly entered an uncontrollable overspeed condition, with vertical descent rates accelerating from 10,000 FPM past 32,000 FPM before the violent ground collision.

Key Investigation Priorities for the NTSB
Locating the Empennage Components: Ground teams are prioritizing the recovery of tail structure fragments, elevator control horns, and pitch trim actuators to determine whether failure was aerodynamic, mechanical, or structural.

Analyzing Trim Jackscrew Position: Recovery crews will inspect the horizontal stabilizer trim actuator jackscrew to determine if an uncommanded runaway pitch condition preceded the structural separation.

Evaluating Atmospheric Stress & Icing: Meteorologists and investigators are analyzing weather radar data to evaluate whether severe convective turbulence or structural ice accumulation induced catastrophic aerodynamic loading at cruise altitude.

When the Civil War broke out, Mary Walker wasn't asking for permission. She was already a doctor, one of the very few women in America who could say that back in 1855. The Army told her women couldn't serve as surgeons. So she showed up anyway and worked for free.

She treated wounded Union soldiers in field hospitals, often close to the fighting. She'd cross into dangerous ground to care for civilians too, and in April 1864 that cost her. Confederate troops captured her and accused her of being a spy. She spent four months locked up in Castle Thunder prison in Richmond before she was traded back in a prisoner exchange.

In November 1865, President Andrew Johnson awarded her the Medal of Honor.

But her story didn't end neatly. In 1917, the government tightened the rules and took the medal back from her and hundreds of others. Mary's answer? She refused to return it. She wore it every single day until she died in 1919.

It took almost 60 more years, but in 1977 President Jimmy Carter restored her medal.

To this day, she is the only woman ever to receive the Medal of Honor.

She was stubborn, fearless, and way ahead of her time. And she never once backed down.

“WE WERE STACKING SO MANY BODIES THAT PATROLS HAD TO GO OUT TO MOVE THEM OFF OUR FIELDS OF FIRE.” — Marine Raider Cody Alford on the Battle of Fallujah on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most intense firsthand accounts of modern urban warfare ever recorded on The Shawn Ryan Show, former Marine Raider and Scout Sniper Cody Alford broke down the brutal house-to-house meatgrinder of Operation Phantom Fury—and the terrifying out-of-body experience he suffered after taking an insurgent sniper bullet directly to the helmet.

In his own words:

“The night prior to going in, my platoon commander walks in and says, ‘Everyone is going to write their death letter.’

I’m 18 years old, sitting there thinking: What do you even write? I wrote a letter to my girlfriend, wrote one to my parents, turned them over to the platoon commander, and that’s when I knew shit was real.

In Fallujah, the brutality of what we were up against was beyond comprehension. The human shields, the mutilations, the sheer volume of combat. We were stacking so many bodies that we had to send patrols out into the street just to drag bodies out of the way because they were blocking our fields of fire.

I remember stepping behind a window frame, slamming in a fresh magazine, and as soon as I pop out to shoot, everything goes black.

A profound exhale left my body, and I hit the deck. That’s when I had this out-of-body experience. It was like a video game glitch—a top-down view looking down at the entire scene. I could see the fighters across the street. I could see my own body lying still. I could see my point man still firing. I saw this blinding light, thinking: I’m f**king dead.

Then suddenly, I got sucked back into my body. I came to curled up in a fetal position with my buddy kicking my leg shouting, ‘Wake up! We thought you were dead!’

The bullet had hit me flush in the helmet.”

The Second Battle of Fallujah stands as the bloodiest, most relentless urban combat the U.S. Marine Corps has fought since the Battle of Huế City in 1968.

“THE POINT MAN FELL AT THE DOORWAY. HE CHARGED IN ANYWAY.” How Navy SEAL Edward Byers Shielded an American Hostage with His Own Body.

On the night of December 8, 2012, a hostage rescue force from SEAL Team 6 inserted into the rugged mountains of eastern Afghanistan on a mission with zero room for error: rescue American physician Dr. Dilip Joseph, who had been kidnapped by Taliban militants and was hours away from being smuggled across the border into Pakistan.

After a grueling four-hour foot patrol through steep terrain, the team reached the isolated target compound in Laghman Province:

As the team approached, an armed sentry alerted fighters inside. Point man Chief Petty Officer Nicolas Checque breached the entrance and was immediately struck by point-blank AK-47 fire and mortally wounded.

Without a second of hesitation, Senior Chief Edward Byers pushed directly through the doorway—the deadly "fatal funnel." He ripped down heavy blankets blocking the threshold, sprinted into the darkened room, and neutralized an armed Taliban fighter.

 Tackling another insurgent to the floor, Byers heard a voice speaking English. Spotting Dr. Joseph in the corner, Byers immediately threw his own body across the doctor, using his plate carrier and physical weight to shield the hostage from heavy incoming gunfire.

 While pinning himself over Dr. Joseph to absorb any stray rounds, Byers noticed another armed guard within arm's reach. With his bare hand, Byers grabbed the insurgent by the throat, pinning him against the wall until his teammates could eliminate the threat.

Dr. Joseph was successfully extracted alive and uninjured. Chief Petty Officer Nicolas Checque made the ultimate sacrifice that night and was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross.

On February 29, 2016, Edward Byers was presented the Medal of Honor, becoming only the sixth Navy SEAL in history to receive the nation’s highest military award for valor.

TRAPPED INSIDE A 1,000-DEGREE INFERNO FOR 90 SECONDS. In March 2001, Phoenix Police Officer Jason Schechterle was stopped at a red light in his Crown Victoria cruiser when a vehicle traveling over 115 mph rear-ended him, rupturing the fuel tank and igniting a blinding fireball. Trapped inside with crumpled doors, he survived fourth-degree burns across 40% of his body, endured over 50 surgeries, and built an unbreakable life out of the ashes.

“I was trapped in a cage of fire for a minute and a half. When I finally woke up from a two-and-a-half-month coma, my face was gone, my hands were severely damaged, and my life as I knew it had vanished. But tragedy doesn't define who you are—your response to it does. There is nothing in this world as powerful as a made-up mind.”

— Officer Jason Schechterle, Phoenix Police Department & Author of Burning Shield

The Incident & The 90-Second Rescue
The 115 MPH Collision: Stopped at an intersection on Thomas Road in Phoenix, Arizona, Officer Jason Schechterle’s patrol vehicle was rear-ended at highway speeds by a driver who had suffered a medical seizure behind the wheel.

 The severe impact crushed the Crown Victoria’s rear crumple zone into the fuel tank, sparking an immediate 1,000-degree gasoline fire that engulfed the passenger cabin and jammed the doors shut.

Phoenix Fire Captain Gary West was nearby when the crash occurred. Armed with only a small dry-chemical extinguisher, he fought through intense heat, forced open the mangled door frame, and pulled Schechterle from the burning cockpit with seconds to spare.

 Schechterle sustained devastating fourth-degree burns across more than 40% of his body, losing his ears, nose, eyelids, and facial skin. Placed into a medically induced coma for two and a half months, he underwent more than 50 surgeries to reconstruct his features and restore eyesight.

Demonstrating extraordinary resilience, Schechterle returned to work with the Phoenix Police Department, authored his autobiography Burning Shield, and became an internationally renowned keynote speaker on overcoming life-altering adversity.

Key Lessons on Resilience & Overcoming Adversity
Focusing on the Response, Not the Circumstance: Pain and trauma are inevitable, but victimhood is a choice. Reframing catastrophic injury into a platform for service enables long-term psychological recovery.

Winning the Internal Battle: Recovery from severe physical trauma is primarily cognitive. Rebuilding daily discipline and maintaining positive internal dialogue prevents despair from taking root.

The Power of First Responder Brotherhood: Schechterle’s survival was made possible by the decisive, selfless courage of a firefighter who entered a raging vehicle fire without full protective gear to save a brother officer.

A Conditional 2-Day Reopening Plan: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented a structured 48-hour timeline under which Iranian naval forces and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) fast-attack craft would stand down from maritime interdictions, allowing commercial tankers to resume transit through the 21-mile-wide chokepoint.

 Tehran’s diplomatic framework requires the United States to immediately halt retaliatory airstrikes, freeze planned operations against Iranian energy terminals, and establish formal security guarantees mediated through ongoing negotiations in Doha, Qatar.

The proposal follows weeks of escalating maritime warfare in which 11 commercial supertankers were struck or damaged by limpet mines, loitering munitions, and drone boats in the Strait of Hormuz, driving maritime insurance premiums to historic highs and threatening roughly 20% of the world's petroleum transit.

The 48-hour window presents a critical crossroads for the administration: defense hawks advocate continuing kinetic strikes to degrade Iran's anti-ship missile sites, while regional Gulf partners and economic advisors urge accepting a ceasefire framework to avert an international energy shock.

Accepting Tehran's terms risks signaling that maritime extortion yields diplomatic leverage, while rejecting the 48-hour off-ramp could trigger protracted naval combat across the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.

Vulnerability of Global Supply Chains: With approximately 850 crude supertankers operating globally, prolonged closures or continuous mine warfare threaten global fertilizer, crude oil, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) distribution networks.

“EVIDENCE INDICATES PARTS OF THE JET BROKE OFF BEFORE IMPACT.” — Federal investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board reveal that the doomed Learjet 60 that crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, likely suffered an in-flight structural breakup at altitude, aligning with dashcam video appearing to show the aircraft plunging nose-first without its T-tail horizontal stabilizer.

“There are indications the aircraft began breaking up prior to impact. We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site... We are asking anyone in the community who locates debris to contact local law enforcement immediately.”

— National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Press Briefing in Palm Beach County

“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence... Mayday, mayday, we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute... We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute... We’re going to crash into the ground.”

— Cockpit transmissions broadcast over Air Traffic Control frequencies moments before impact

Aerodynamic & Forensic Breakdown
The In-Flight Breakup Finding: During their initial media briefing in Palm Beach County, NTSB investigators confirmed that the Learjet 60 began shedding components prior to striking the ground, officially expanding the search radius across residential neighborhoods miles away from the primary impact crater.

The Missing Horizontal Stabilizer: Close-up frame analysis of civilian dashcam footage captured seconds before impact appears to show the aircraft's T-tail fuselage cleanly sheared off, missing the entire horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly that controls aircraft pitch.

Why Loss of the Stabilizer is Fatal: On swept-wing, T-tail jets like the Learjet 60, the horizontal stabilizer generates continuous downward aerodynamic force to counter the natural forward center of gravity. If the stabilizer separates due to severe structural flutter, pitch trim runaway, or aerodynamic over-stress, the aircraft immediately lawn-darts into a near-vertical terminal dive that is physically impossible to pull out of, regardless of pilot yoke input.

The Escalating Mayday Telemetry: Flight tracking telemetry and ATC recordings show the crew encountered severe weather and icing while climbing through 8,700 feet. The aircraft suddenly entered an uncontrollable overspeed condition, with vertical descent rates accelerating from 10,000 FPM past 32,000 FPM before the violent ground collision.

Key Investigation Priorities for the NTSB
Locating the Empennage Components: Ground teams are prioritizing the recovery of tail structure fragments, elevator control horns, and pitch trim actuators to determine whether failure was aerodynamic, mechanical, or structural.

Analyzing Trim Jackscrew Position: Recovery crews will inspect the horizontal stabilizer trim actuator jackscrew to determine if an uncommanded runaway pitch condition preceded the structural separation.

Evaluating Atmospheric Stress & Icing: Meteorologists and investigators are analyzing weather radar data to evaluate whether severe convective turbulence or structural ice accumulation induced catastrophic aerodynamic loading at cruise altitude.

When then-Pfc. Adlesperger and his squad approached a house on Nov. 10, 2004, in the treacherous city of Fallujah. They entered into one of the most difficult and dangerous battlefield situations: they faced an entrenched enemy in an urban setting, with an entrenched machine gun.

As they entered the house, a volley of insurgent fire and grenades rained down upon them, immediately killing Adlesperger’s point man and injuring two others. Without pause, Adlesperger took control and moved out front, despite receiving minor wounds. As Adlesperger began firing back from the point position, he became the main target of enemy fire – but, with most of his squad pinned down by insurgent fire, he had no choice but to push forward on his own.

Adlesperger single-handedly cleared the stairs to the rooftop, which allowed the unit to move injured Marines upstairs to receive medical attention. And as U.S. forces gathered for a major assault on the building, Adlesperger, still inside, began moving from one spot to another, eliminating enemies in close quarters or forcing them to move out of entrenched positions to areas where U.S. forces were waiting.

Finally, an assault vehicle broke through a wall on the main floor. Adlesperger rejoined his platoon and demanded to take point for the final attack on the entrenched machine gun. He entered the courtyard first and eliminated the final enemy at close range. By the end of the battle, Adlesperger was credited with having killed at least 11 insurgents.

One month later, Adlesperger was killed while clearing other houses in Fallujah. For his actions on Nov. 10, 2004, Adlesperger will be posthumously awarded the Navy Cross on April 13, 2007.

U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel Kathryn Van Auken and Major Lauralee Flannery were awarded the Bronze Star with "V" for valor for their sustained courage and heroic performance of duties while serving in Operation Iraqi Freedom.

Van Auken and Flannery had been serving together in Iraq in support of a Kuwait Exploitation Team's objective to secure, safe guard and assist a Kuwait forensic team in the recovery of the remains of Kuwaiti Prisoners of War and Missing from the end of the 1991 Gulf War.

Van Auken and Flannery were traveling together in the lead vehicle on February 14, 2007. They had been tasked with escorting the Kuwait Forensic Team's convoy of 12 vehicles.

It was approximately 7:30 a.m. when the middle four vehicles of the convoy were hit with the largest planned improvised explosive device (IED) attack that had been recorded up until that time.

Ten daisy-chained 155mm mortar rounds had been buried under the raised causeway they were traveling on, south of Razzazah Lake in the vicinity of Karbala, Iraq.

When these IEDs exploded three vehicles were destroyed, and passengers -- disoriented and bleeding -- began exiting their vehicles.

We both exited our vehicle," Van Auken said. "[MAJ Flannery] headed east and I headed west trying to gather up everyone and secure both ends of the roadway against secondary attacks."

As team leader, Van Auken deployed rapidly, undertaking a multiplicity of actions, quickly radioing instructions to move all vehicles through the smoke and debris and to follow her vehicle into safety away from the IED site to avoid secondary devices.

In this highly fluid situation, vehicles became disabled. Van Auken and Flannery quickly ordered the destroyed vehicles to be pushed out of the kill zone by follow on vehicles in the convoy in order to assemble the team and get everyone to a safe and secure distance.

Van Auken then maneuvered the front column of Polish security elements and Korean Engineer vehicles into security postures along west side of the raised causeway with great speed and determination gaining the advantage against any follow-on IED or possible ambush.

Both soldiers reacted fearlessly and without hesitation, running alone down the west end of the roadway to halt any oncoming traffic, orienting Iraqi vehicles to block the road, dismissing large crowds gathering, and re-positioning Polish security forces to assist.

The team provided medical assistance to their Kuwaiti team members who had been badly cut with glass and debris, and who were vomiting and shaking on the side of the road from the shocking experience.

Their actions provided an example of urgency and purpose to fellow coalition forces, and their courage under fire unquestionably saved the lives of coalition forces, particularly the civilians in their charge.

" We are battle buddies to the end," Van Auken said.

When the Civil War broke out, Mary Walker wasn't asking for permission. She was already a doctor, one of the very few women in America who could say that back in 1855. The Army told her women couldn't serve as surgeons. So she showed up anyway and worked for free.

She treated wounded Union soldiers in field hospitals, often close to the fighting. She'd cross into dangerous ground to care for civilians too, and in April 1864 that cost her. Confederate troops captured her and accused her of being a spy. She spent four months locked up in Castle Thunder prison in Richmond before she was traded back in a prisoner exchange.

In November 1865, President Andrew Johnson awarded her the Medal of Honor.

But her story didn't end neatly. In 1917, the government tightened the rules and took the medal back from her and hundreds of others. Mary's answer? She refused to return it. She wore it every single day until she died in 1919.

It took almost 60 more years, but in 1977 President Jimmy Carter restored her medal.

To this day, she is the only woman ever to receive the Medal of Honor.

She was stubborn, fearless, and way ahead of her time. And she never once backed down.

Rest easy, Dr. Walker. 🇺🇸

Key Details from the Crash Investigation
The Catastrophic Descent: Flight tracking data released by Flightradar24 indicates the twin-engine Learjet 60 (tail number N722BD) had departed South Florida en route to the Bahamas when it suddenly rolled past 60 degrees of bank and entered an uncontrolled vertical dive exceeding 32,000 feet per minute, erupting into a massive fireball upon impact in a roadway near Lantana.

Prisoners of war have tried everything to escape, but few plans were as patient — or as strange — as Benjamin Purcell's. Held in a North Vietnamese prison camp, the Army officer spent months secretly drilling tiny holes into his cell door, a little at a time, always watching for the guards. His early-warning system was a chicken he had trained to react whenever anyone approached.

On December 7, 1969, he slipped through the opening and spent nearly ten hours outside the wire — he even caught a bicycle ride toward Hanoi — before being recaptured and thrown into stocks for two weeks. He would not see freedom until 1973. He retired as a colonel, carrying one of the most remarkable escape stories of the Vietnam War: no tools, no help, just patience, nerve, and a chicken.

“POLITICIZATION IS PUSHING TROOPS TOWARD THE EXIT.” — A national survey of service members, veterans, and military families reveals that 53% of active-duty troops say increasing political interference and partisan polarization within the armed forces are driving them to leave service early—more than double the number citing pay or benefits.

“Veterans know what real leadership looks like: you take care of the people under your command, and you keep politics out of the mission. For too long, political leaders have treated the military as a partisan backdrop rather than protecting the core readiness of the force.”

— Jose Vasquez, U.S. Army Veteran & Executive Director of Common Defense

Key Findings from the National Survey
Politicization Outpaces Pay and Quality of Life: According to the latest national survey conducted by Common Defense, 53% of active-duty respondents report that growing political polarization makes them want to separate sooner, while only 5% say it encourages them to stay. By comparison, just 26% cited compensation and benefits as their primary retention concern.

Bipartisan Concern Across the Ranks: Frustration over politicization crosses traditional party affiliations. Among Republican-identifying service members and veterans, 72% agree that military families are being sidelined by political agendas, and 63% state defense policies are increasingly engineered for short-term domestic political gain.

Widespread Institutional Discontent: Over 79% of surveyed troops, veterans, and military dependents feel that civilian leadership and broader society are leaving the military community behind, with 74% expressing disapproval of how Congress oversees defense affairs.

Protecting the Apolitical Tradition: The survey highlighted strong opposition to using armed forces for domestic political functions: 55% of respondents reject deploying active-duty troops to monitor civilian polling stations or participate in domestic civil policing, reaffirming the constitutional standard of an apolitical military.

Strategic Implications for Retention & Readiness
Compounding the Recruiting Crisis: As all branches battle historically challenging recruiting environments, losing experienced mid-career NCOs and junior officers over political fatigue threatens institutional knowledge, unit cohesion, and technical combat capabilities.

Erosion of Public Trust: Decades of defense polling demonstrate that public confidence in the armed forces relies directly on its strictly non-partisan status. Partisan debates over command appointments, social messaging, and foreign policy rhetoric risk undermining that foundational trust.

Mission Focus vs. Narrative Battles: Frontline leaders emphasize that unit effectiveness hinges on warfighting competency, tactical drills, and equipment readiness, warning that culture-war distractions degrade morale in operational formations.

Staff Sgt. Jeffery M. Dawson earned the Distinguished Service Cross while deployed to Afghanistan with the 28th EOD Company (Airborne) in support of the U.S. Army's elite 75th Ranger Regiment.

Dawson said the mission in Afghanistan on Oct. 5, 2013, was supposed to be routine.

"That mission started out the same as every mission. The IED (Improvised Explosive Device) threat was low, and it was supposed to be a quick, easy target," said Dawson. "Upon infiltration, everything changed in minutes."

During the mission at a remote enemy compound, a fleeing insurgent detonated an explosive, killing himself and the team's multi-purpose canine Jani.

Dawson then realized that his team was surrounded by IEDs.

"Being the only EOD tech on the objective, it was up to me to clear medical personnel to the wounded and clear to all other personnel to get them to safety," said Dawson.

Despite being wounded by two separate explosions, Dawson halted the mission, disarmed the improvised explosive devices, and aided in the evacuation of dead and wounded Soldiers.

Navigating the chaotic situation in limited visibility for more than two hours, Dawson exposed himself to grave danger while locating three confirmed pressure plate IEDs and an additional six suspected devices, the award citation said.

"In any situation like that, you always revert back to training and stick with what you know," said Dawson, a Coalville, Utah native who has served in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Dawson said he was inspired by the dedication of his fellow Soldiers who braved the explosive-ridden battlefield to recover their fallen and wounded teammates.

"I remember looking around at all the devastation and seeing American flags draped over casualties in an effort to help keep them warm," said Dawson.

The staff sergeant said he was surprised to be put in for the medal, second only to the Medal of Honor.

"When I got back to camp, people were coming up to me and shaking my hand and hugging me telling me that they heard great things about me," said Dawson. "I kept thinking to myself that I was just doing my job

The Fort Bragg, North Carolina-based 28th EOD Company (Airborne) is part of the 192nd EOD Battalion, 52nd EOD Group, 20th CBRNE Command (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, Explosives), the only Defense Department formation that combats global CBRNE threats.

According to 28th EOD Company Commander Capt. Taylor J. Duren, his Soldiers conduct rigorous training to stay ready to jump out of airplanes and defuse explosive devices. Duren said his Soldiers regularly serve with the 75th Ranger Regiment, the U.S. Army's premier direct-action raid force.

"(The medal) highlights the relationship we have with the 75th Ranger Regiment since they are the ones who submitted (Staff Sergeant) Dawson's Distinguished Service Cross," said Duren.

Duren said the medal demonstrates the high caliber of the Soldiers serving in his one-of-a-kind company.

"What makes us truly unique is the level of professionalism each Soldier depicts in this company," said Duren, a native of Columbia, South Carolina, who has deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan.

"This award pays tribute to the level of training we put into the Soldiers hand-selected to serve in this company and their dedication to mission success," said Duren.

“10 TO 11 MONTHS AWAY FROM HOME IS THE NEW NORMAL.” Navy Leadership Warns Sailors Traditional 7-Month Deployments Are Years Away.

For decades, a typical U.S. Navy carrier strike group deployment lasted six to seven months. But amid relentless operational demands in the Middle East and a severe shipyard maintenance backlog, the Pentagon is delivering a hard truth to sailors and their families: prepare for 10-to-11-month tours at sea.

According to naval leadership reports, returning to predictable seven-month deployment schedules could still be several years away as the fleet struggles to balance global commitments with limited ready ships.

Why Carrier Tours Keep Getting Extended:

 Continuous combat operations in the Red Sea countering Houthi missile and drone swarms have forced strike groups including the USS Gerald R. Ford (326 days at sea) and the USS Abraham Lincoln (over 320 days) into historic, repeated deployment extensions.

“Sorry, guys, I can't keep going.”

Those were the words of Lance Cpl. Brady A. Gustafson to the Marines in his vehicle as he was pulled away from his smoking machine gun minutes after his platoon was ambushed July 21, 2008, by withering enemy fire in Shewan, Afghanistan.

Nobody blamed Gustafson, 21, an infantryman with 2nd Platoon, Company G, 2nd Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, for not being able to continue the fight, since the opening volley on the Marine mounted patrol included a rocket-propelled grenade that pierced the shell of the mine-resistant armor-protected vehicle in which Gustafson was manning the turret gun.

That RPG severed Gustafson's right leg, and yet he had the presence of mind to locate the enemy positions and place well-aimed machine gun fire on them, providing cover fire for the Marines in his platoon.

For his actions that day last year, Gustafson was awarded the Navy Cross and meritoriously promoted to corporal by Maj. Gen. Thomas D. Waldhauser, commanding general, 1st Marine Division, at a ceremony Mar. 27 at Lance Cpl. Torrey L. Gray Field at Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms, Calif.
“What I like about today is that this is an opportunity to honor a Marine who had the humility, courage, presence of mind and camaraderie to keep going,” said Lt. Col. Richard D. Hall, the former commanding officer of 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines,
while they were deployed to Afghanistan in support of Operation Enduring Freedom – noting that Gustafson was more concerned about the welfare of his brother Marines than his own safety.
“He represents what is best about the human spirit. You can't buy that kind of human altruism.”

The Navy Cross is the highest honor specific to the Naval services and the second highest award in the U.S. military. Gustafson is just the 18th Marine to earn the award since the beginning of the Global War on Terror.

The Marines of 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines battled elements of Taliban and Islamist extremists in the Helmand and Farah provinces of Afghanistan.

Gustafson and Company G were patrolling in the village of Shewan, noted as a haven for insurgents, when they were ambushed from multiple positions by insurgents with RPGs and small-arms fire, according to the award citation for the Navy Cross.

After the RPG pierced the side of Gustafson's MRAP and struck him in the leg, causing the severe injury, he stayed focused and identified enemy firing positions, which he engaged with accurate machine-gun fire.

He noticed that the vehicle to his rear had become disabled by another RPG and instructed his MRAP driver to push the hobbled vehicle out of the “kill-zone.”

By doing so, Gustafson's MRAP became shrouded in fire. Through all this, Gustafson continued to direct fire at the enemy positions, suppressing their attacks and allowing the Marines to continue to engage the insurgents.

“Of every Marine I talked to, they all said if they had been hit in the leg with an RPG, the last thing they'd be thinking about is staying in the turret,” said 1st Lt. Andrew S. Bohn, 25, platoon commander of 2nd Plt., from Davis, Calif., and an occupant of the second vehicle that Gustafson directed to be pushed out of the line of fire.

Without that presence of mind, Bohn and the four other Marines from that vehicle may not have made it out of the ambush alive.

Only after firing more than 400 rounds, and reloading twice, did Gustafson permit combat aid-givers to remove him from the turret to apply medical treatment to his significant injuries. Lance Cpl. Cody Comstock, a member of Gustafson's platoon, applied his Combat Life Saver Course knowledge to the situation, wrapping a tourniquet around Gustafson's leg and dressing the wound while Gustafson was still in the turret.

“All of the lance corporals were going off their training in immediate action - nobody panicked,” said Bohn of his Marines. “There was a much-superior sized force attacking us, and there was only one (noncommissioned officer) in the platoon.”

After the action was over, Bohn recommended Gustafson for the Silver Star, the third highest combat award for valor, but Hall disagreed.

“My awards policy has always been strict (and) conservative,” said Hall, from Mankato, Minn. The former battalion commander noted that the deployment put all of his Marines in harsh conditions, and yet so many of the Marines excelled at operating at a high level that the “extraordinary became ordinary.”
Even so, Gustafson's actions were special.

“After reviewing what he did, even considering my awards policy and all the actions of 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines, it was easy, to me, to submit his award as a Navy Cross,” Hall said.

Gustafson, from Eagan, Minn., has a long road to recovery and walks with a pronounced limp on his prosthetic right leg. The fact he suffered traumatic injury made his family even more grateful for his return.

“(The Navy Cross) is the icing on the cake for us, but we know that Brady didn't do this for the awards,” said Rick Gustafson, father to the Marine hero and an Air Force retiree. “We're very thankful we have him here today. That's our primary emotion.”

According to his parents, Gustafson intends to buy a home in his native Minnesota and attend college somewhere near home.

“He recognizes the importance and honor of the award, but at the same time, he feels funny about being recognized,” said Gustafson's mother, Kim, about her son's quiet, unassuming manner and reluctance to stand in front of the hundreds of Marines, guests and media at the ceremony. “He was just fighting for
his guys' lives."

MARINE CORPS BASE CAMP PENDLETON, Calif. (5/18/2012) – Corporal Christopher B. Farias, 1st Battalion, 11th Marine Regiment, was awarded the nation's second highest award for bravery during a ceremony here, May 18.

Under Secretary of the Navy Robert Work presented the Navy Cross to Farias for heroic actions while serving as an assistant squad leader in the Kajaki district of Afghanistan on Oct. 5, 2010.

After Farias, a native of La Porte, Texas, arrived in Afghanistan, the commanding officer pulled the Marines together and mentioned they would protect the Kajaki Dam and relieve British forces at the front line.

“To find out that we're surrounded in three different areas by Taliban fighters, that's telling me that we're definitely on our own on this one,” Farias explained.

Farias was excited to do infantry missions because he had experience in Iraq with foot patrols and security and felt the Marines in his squad were well trained and confident in their abilities to complete their mission on the northern frontier of the Marines' battlespace in Kajaki.

During the night of the fight, Farias requested to go on the mission because he enjoyed patrolling, he said. The Marines planned to set up an ambush against enemy forces moving throughout the area.

While preparing for the attack, the Marines received reports that enemy fighters called for reinforcements, including a “special weapon,” a 73-millimeter recoilless rifle. The rounds are larger than the rounds of some mortar systems.

Farias and the squad heard an explosion and received enemy fire from three positions in a vicious ambush. Several Marines lay wounded by the recoilless rifle, and insurgent forces adjusted their fires and continued to shoot into the Marines' position.
 

“These guys were tactically and strategically smart,” said Farias. They were well trained. To have guys who can fight just like you... they know how to maneuver, they know how to set you up for a proper ambush... to fight an enemy like that, it's pretty insane.”

Farias suffered a concussion and fragmentation wounds in the neck and shoulder and received hasty treatment for his wounds before directing medical care for the other Marines. After securing the wounded, Farias climbed to a rooftop and controlled the fire of the machine guns to suppress enemy positions.

The suppressive fires kept the enemy down and allowed the squad to treat the wounded, clear a landing zone, and evacuate the casualties. Farias remained with his squad until an airstrike ended the engagement.

Afterward, Farias walked more than 2,000 meters back to a ground evacuation site. His neck was bleeding, and he felt drained due to blood loss, he remembered.

“As we were walking back, that's when I started feeling every bit of pain possible,” recounted Farias. “I ended up realizing my right arm would not move. I could not move it to save my life if I wanted to.”
Farias was recommended for a Silver Star, which was upgraded to a Navy Cross. The Marines of 1st Battalion, 11th Marine Regiment formed on the parade deck with M777 lightweight howitzers on display. Farias said he was honored to receive the award on behalf of his Marines and the unit.

“I don't see it as actually for me,” Farias said. “I see it as for India Battery, but for me to stand there and be a representation for India Battery for that award... it's a shocker.”

I could see the fighters across the street. I could see my own body lying still. I could see my point man still firing. I saw this blinding light, thinking: I’m f**king dead.

Then suddenly, I got sucked back into my body. I came to curled up in a fetal position with my buddy kicking my leg shouting, ‘Wake up! We thought you were dead!’
