The President of the United States of America, authorized by Act of Congress July 9, 1918, takes pleasure in presenting the Navy Cross to Hospital Corpsman First Class Justin A. Wilson, United States Navy, for extraordinary heroism while serving as Special Amphibious Reconnaissance Corpsman, U.S. Marine Corps Forces, Special Operations Command in support of Operation ENDURING FREEDOM. On 28 September 2011 while on a mounted patrol, Petty Officer Wilson volunteered to accompany the team’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) Technician to clear an improvised explosive device (IED) from an Afghan Local Police checkpoint. As the EOD Tech entered the checkpoint’s barriers to inspect the IED, there was a large explosion. Despite being disoriented by the dust and overpressure from the blast, and knowing the enemy’s tactic of emplacing multiple IEDs in proximity, Petty Officer Wilson immediately left the safety of his position and searched the checkpoint until he located the severely wounded EOD Tech. Two other team members arrived and were helping move the casualty when a second device exploded, severely wounding Petty Officer Wilson and mortally wounding the others. Ignoring the pain of his own injuries, Petty Officer Wilson focused solely on treating his fellow team members. He dragged one outside the checkpoint and rendered aid until he succumbed, and then searched for the other casualties, who had been blown over the barriers by the second blast. Only after confirming they were already dead did he allow treatment of his own wounds. By his decisive actions, bold initiative, and complete dedication to duty, Petty Officer Wilson reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service.

DEFINITION OF F*CK AROUND AND FIND OUT “DOES PROTESTING GIVE YOU THE RIGHT TO BLOCK FEDERAL AGENTS?”

Footage recorded outside the ICE processing facility in Broadview, Illinois, has triggered a nationwide debate over lawful protest, federal authority, and the boundaries of reasonable force.

In the viral clip, an activist holding an umbrella stands squarely in front of an official ICE SUV, refusing repeated directives to clear the driveway during an active enforcement operation. A federal agent in tactical gear steps up, shoves her aside to clear the vehicle’s path, and she falls onto the wet asphalt before agents proceed.

Critics and civil rights activists were quick to label the shove police brutality, citing 18 U.S.C. § 242 (deprivation of rights under color of law) and arguing the force used was unnecessary against a non-violent demonstrator.

Federal law enforcement advocates and legal analysts counter that intentional physical obstruction of official government vehicles constitutes interference under 18 U.S.C. § 111. Under established federal standards, officers are legally authorized to apply proportional, minimal physical force to remove active barricades and hazards from transit paths so lawful operations can continue safely.

Public reactions from viewers who analyzed the unedited footage:

“The right to protest doesn’t include blocking traffic, breaking laws, and obstructing federal vehicles.”

“That was measured, reasonable force to clear an active obstruction. When someone repeatedly refuses lawful orders to step aside, officers have an obligation to clear the roadway.”

“Protest rights protect speech, but they do not provide a license to physically impede law enforcement operations.”

Federal agents have a statutory duty to carry out operations directed by Congress. While peaceful assembly remains constitutionally protected, physically blocking official vehicles escalates a demonstration into an active obstruction hazard.

Where do you draw the line? Was the officer’s action a lawful, necessary clearance to maintain operations, or did it cross into excessive force?

“PULLED FROM THE WATER, THEN STRIPPED OF HIS G.I. BILL.” — Navy Moves to Discharge 19-Year-Old Carrier Sailor After Overboard Crisis.

A fierce debate over mental health, deployment burnout, and military discipline has erupted after the U.S. Navy moved to administratively discharge a 19-year-old sailor who survived jumping overboard from an aircraft carrier.

Navy Airman Nicholas McKelvey was deployed aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) during an grueling deployment in the Middle East and Red Sea, where the carrier strike group spent over 250 consecutive days at sea fending off continuous drone and missile threats.

Following an apparent mental health crisis, McKelvey went overboard into the ocean and was miraculously rescued by shipboard search-and-rescue teams.

But instead of medical treatment and an honorable administrative separation, naval authorities moved to process him for separation on grounds of alleged "malingering"—issuing a General Discharge Under Honorable Conditions.

The Key Points Driving the Backlash:

• Loss of Education Benefits: Under federal law, receiving a General Discharge permanently strips a veteran of their Post-9/11 G.I. Bill, eliminating tens of thousands of dollars in earned college tuition and housing allowances.

• The Strain of 250+ Days at Sea: Veteran advocates point out that junior enlisted personnel on modern carrier deployments face historic operational tempos, extreme sleep deprivation, and minimal mental health infrastructure while operating in active combat zones.

Military leadership maintains that deliberately jumping overboard endangers helicopter rescue crews, diverts combat strike groups from primary missions, and undermines good order and discipline.

When a junior service member suffers a severe breakdown during an extended combat deployment, should the military treat it as a medical emergency warranting an Honorable medical separation, or is administrative discipline necessary to deter copycat incidents?
